4. Wavelets

CNRS & DMA, École Normale Supérieure

Chapter PDF · Complete book

Signals contain broad trends and localized details that occur at different scales. Separating these components produces representations suited to compression and denoising, while allowing each scale to be processed efficiently. We build orthonormal wavelet bases from nested approximation spaces, derive fast decomposition and reconstruction algorithms in one and two dimensions, and explain how filter design controls localization, smoothness, and cancellation of polynomials.

The reference for this chapter is [23].

Let θ∈L2(R)\theta\in L^2(\mathbb{R})θ∈L2(R). Its translates {θ(⋅−n)}n∈Z\{\theta(\cdot-n)\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}{θ(⋅−n)}n∈Z​ are orthonormal if and only if

A(ω):=∑k∣θ^(ω−2πk)∣2=1for almost every ω.A(\omega) \mathrel{:=}\sum_{k} |\hat \theta(\omega-2\pi k)|^2 = 1 \quad\text{for almost every }\omega.A(ω):=k∑​∣θ^(ω−2πk)∣2=1for almost every ω.

If there exist 0<a⩽b<+∞0 < a \leqslant b <+\infty0<a⩽b<+∞ such that a⩽A(ω)⩽ba \leqslant A(\omega) \leqslant ba⩽A(ω)⩽b almost everywhere, then φ\varphiφ defined by

φ^(ω)=θ^(ω)A(ω)\hat\varphi(\omega) = \frac{\hat\theta(\omega)}{\sqrt{A(\omega)}}φ^​(ω)=A(ω)​θ^(ω)​

is such that {φ(⋅−n)}n∈Z\{\varphi(\cdot-n)\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}{φ(⋅−n)}n∈Z​ is an orthonormal basis of Span‾{θ(⋅−n)}n∈Z\overline{\mathop{\mathrm{Span}}}\{\theta(\cdot-n)\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}Span​{θ(⋅−n)}n∈Z​.

Proof

The family {θ(⋅−n)}n∈Z\{\theta(\cdot-n)\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}{θ(⋅−n)}n∈Z​ is orthonormal if and only if

⟨θ, θ(⋅−n)⟩=(θ⋆θˉ)(n)=δ0,n:={1ifn=0,0otherwise.\langle \theta,\,\theta(\cdot-n)\rangle = (\theta\star \bar\theta)(n) = \delta_{0,n} \mathrel{:=} \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 1 \quad \text{if} \quad n=0, \\ 0 \quad\text{otherwise.} \end{array} \right.⟨θ,θ(⋅−n)⟩=(θ⋆θˉ)(n)=δ0,n​:={1ifn=0,0otherwise.​

where θˉ(x)=θ(−x)‾\bar\theta(x)=\overline{\theta(-x)}θˉ(x)=θ(−x)​ and δ0\delta_0δ0​ is the discrete Dirac vector.

By Tonelli’s theorem and Plancherel’s identity, A∈L1(T)A\in L^1(\mathbb{T})A∈L1(T). Its Fourier coefficients are

12π∫02πA(ω)e−inω dω=12π∫R∣θ^(ω)∣2e−inω dω=⟨θ, θ(⋅+n)⟩.\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}A(\omega)e^{-\mathrm{i}n\omega}\,\mathrm{d}\omega &=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_\mathbb{R}|\hat\theta(\omega)|^2e^{-\mathrm{i}n\omega}\,\mathrm{d}\omega\\ &=\langle \theta,\,\theta(\cdot+n)\rangle. \end{aligned}2π1​∫02π​A(ω)e−inωdω​=2π1​∫R​∣θ^(ω)∣2e−inωdω=⟨θ,θ(⋅+n)⟩.​

Thus the translates are orthonormal exactly when the Fourier coefficients of AAA are those of the constant function 1. Uniqueness of Fourier coefficients in L1(T)L^1(\mathbb{T})L1(T) gives A=1A=1A=1 almost everywhere.

Since AAA is 2π2\pi2π-periodic, normalization by the bounded function 1/A(ω)1/\sqrt{A(\omega)}1/A(ω)​ gives ∑k∣φ^(ω−2πk)∣2=1\sum_{k} |\hat \varphi(\omega-2\pi k)|^2 = 1∑k​∣φ^​(ω−2πk)∣2=1. It remains to check equality of the closed spans. Approximate the periodic multipliers 1/A1/\sqrt A1/A​ and A\sqrt AA​ by trigonometric polynomials in L2(T)L^2(\mathbb{T})L2(T). The bounds a⩽A⩽ba\leqslant A\leqslant ba⩽A⩽b show that the corresponding products with θ^\hat\thetaθ^ and φ^\hat\varphiφ^​ converge in L2(R)L^2(\mathbb{R})L2(R). Inverting the Fourier transform expresses each generator as an L2L^2L2 limit of finite linear combinations of translates of the other.

Spline interpolation provides a typical application. For example, cubic splines are generated by translates of a box-spline function θ\thetaθ, which is a compactly supported piecewise polynomial.

As in (1.6), the periodization of f∈L1(R)f \in L^1(\mathbb{R})f∈L1(R) is

fP=∑n∈Zf(⋅−n)∈L1(T).f^P = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} f(\cdot-n) \in L^1(\mathbb{T}).fP=n∈Z∑​f(⋅−n)∈L1(T).

For an integer coarsest level j0⩽0j_0\leqslant 0j0​⩽0, this gives the family

{ψj,nP  ;  j⩽j0,0⩽n<2−j}∪{φj0,nP  ;  0⩽n<2−j0}.\left\{ \psi_{j,n}^P \;;\; j \leqslant j_0, 0 \leqslant n < 2^{-j} \right\} \cup \left\{ \varphi_{j_0,n}^P \;;\; 0 \leqslant n < 2^{-j_0} \right\} .{ψj,nP​;j⩽j0​,0⩽n<2−j}∪{φj0​,nP​;0⩽n<2−j0​}.

which is an orthonormal basis of L2(T)L^2(\mathbb{T})L2(T), illustrated in Figure 4.7.

4.4 Fast Wavelet Transform¶

4.4.1 Discretization¶

We now work over R/Z\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}R/Z.

We assume access to a discrete signal aJ∈RNa_J \in \mathbb{R}^NaJ​∈RN with N=2−JN = 2^{-J}N=2−J at a fixed scale 2J2^J2J, whose entries are inner products with the scaling functions, i.e.

∀ n∈{0,…,N−1},aJ,n=⟨f, φJ,nP⟩≈2J/2f(2Jn),(4.5)\forall \,n\in \{0,\ldots,N-1\}, \quad a_{J,n} = \langle f,\,\varphi_{J,n}^P\rangle \approx 2^{J/2}f(2^Jn), \tag{4.5}∀n∈{0,…,N−1},aJ,n​=⟨f,φJ,nP​⟩≈2J/2f(2Jn),(4.5)

for the underlying continuous function fff. The approximation uses the normalization ∫φ=1\int\varphi=1∫φ=1. The equality assumes that acquisition gives exact access to PVJfP_{V_J}fPVJ​​f, much as Shannon sampling assumes bandlimiting. This model is reasonable when the scaling functions (φJ,n)n(\varphi_{J,n})_n(φJ,n​)n​ approximate the acquisition device’s point-spread function. Preprocessing the measurements can sometimes improve agreement with (4.5).

Starting from aJa_JaJ​, the discrete wavelet transform computes the coefficients

∀ j∈{J+1,J+2,…,0},∀ n∈[ ⁣[0,2−j−1] ⁣],aj,n:=⟨f, φj,nP⟩,anddj,n:=⟨f, ψj,nP⟩\forall \,j \in \{J+1,J+2, \ldots, 0\}, \quad \forall \,n \in \lbrack\!\lbrack 0,2^{-j}-1\rbrack\!\rbrack, \quad a_{j,n} \mathrel{:=}\langle f,\,\varphi_{j,n}^P\rangle, \quad \text{and} \quad d_{j,n} \mathrel{:=}\langle f,\,\psi_{j,n}^P\rangle∀j∈{J+1,J+2,…,0},∀n∈[[0,2−j−1]],aj,n​:=⟨f,φj,nP​⟩,anddj,n​:=⟨f,ψj,nP​⟩

in order of increasing jjj. After an approximation vector aja_jaj​ has been used to compute the next scale, it can be discarded; the detail vectors djd_jdj​ are retained.

The forward discrete wavelet transform on a bounded domain is thus the orthogonal finite-dimensional map

aJ∈RN⟼{dj,n  ;  J<j⩽0, 0⩽n<2−j}∪{a0∈R}.a_J \in \mathbb{R}^N \longmapsto \left\{ d_{j,n} \;;\; J<j\leqslant 0,\ 0\leqslant n<2^{-j} \right\} \cup \{a_0 \in \mathbb{R}\}.aJ​∈RN⟼{dj,n​;J<j⩽0, 0⩽n<2−j}∪{a0​∈R}.

By orthogonality, the inverse transform is the adjoint.

4.4.2 Forward Fast Wavelet Transform (FWT)¶

The algorithm applies a sequence of elementary operators

∀ j=J+1,…,0,(aj,dj)=Wj(aj−1)whereWj:R2−j+1→R2−j×R2−j(4.6)\forall \,j = J+1, \ldots, 0, \quad (a_{j},d_{j}) = \mathcal{W}_j(a_{j-1}) \quad \text{where} \quad \mathcal{W}_j : \mathbb{R}^{2^{-j+1}} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{2^{-j}} \times \mathbb{R}^{2^{-j}} \tag{4.6}∀j=J+1,…,0,(aj​,dj​)=Wj​(aj−1​)whereWj​:R2−j+1→R2−j×R2−j(4.6)

There are ∣J∣=log⁡2(N)|J|=\log_2(N)∣J∣=log2​(N) steps. Each Wj\mathcal{W}_jWj​ changes coordinates between orthonormal bases and is therefore orthogonal.

To describe the algorithm for Wj\mathcal{W}_jWj​, we introduce the filter coefficients h,g∈RZh,g \in \mathbb{R}^\mathbb{Z}h,g∈RZ

hn:=12⟨φ(⋅/2), φ(⋅−n)⟩andgn:=12⟨ψ(⋅/2), φ(⋅−n)⟩.(4.7)h_n \mathrel{:=}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \langle \varphi(\cdot/2) ,\,\varphi(\cdot-n)\rangle \quad \text{and} \quad g_n \mathrel{:=}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \langle \psi(\cdot/2) ,\,\varphi(\cdot-n)\rangle. \tag{4.7}hn​:=2​1​⟨φ(⋅/2),φ(⋅−n)⟩andgn​:=2​1​⟨ψ(⋅/2),φ(⋅−n)⟩.(4.7)

We denote by ↓2:RK→RK/2\downarrow_2 : \mathbb{R}^K \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{K/2}↓2​:RK→RK/2 the subsampling operator by a factor of 2, i.e.

u↓2:=(u0,u2,u4,…,uK−2).u\downarrow_2 \mathrel{:=}(u_0,u_2,u_4,\ldots,u_{K-2}).u↓2​:=(u0​,u2​,u4​,…,uK−2​).

One has

4.5 2-D Wavelets¶

4.5.1 Anisotropic Wavelets¶

The anisotropic basis on T2\mathbb{T}^2T2 is the tensor product of the complete one-dimensional periodized basis B\mathcal BB (including its coarsest scaling functions):

{b1⊗b2:b1,b2∈B}.\{b_1\otimes b_2:b_1,b_2\in\mathcal B\}.{b1​⊗b2​:b1​,b2​∈B}.

Its wavelet–wavelet elements have the form

ψ(j1,j2),(n1,n2)(x1,x2)=ψj1,n1P(x1)ψj2,n2P(x2).(4.12)\psi_{(j_1,j_2),(n_1,n_2)}(x_1,x_2) =\psi_{j_1,n_1}^{P}(x_1)\psi_{j_2,n_2}^{P}(x_2). \tag{4.12}ψ(j1​,j2​),(n1​,n2​)​(x1​,x2​)=ψj1​,n1​P​(x1​)ψj2​,n2​P​(x2​).(4.12)

The basis also includes wavelet–scaling, scaling–wavelet, and scaling–scaling products. The anisotropic 2-D transform follows the same separable construction as the 2-D FFT in Section 2.5.2. Treat the image aJ∈R2−J×2−Ja_J \in \mathbb{R}^{2^{-J} \times 2^{-J}}aJ​∈R2−J×2−J as a matrix, apply the 1-D FWT to each row, and then apply it to each column. The total cost is O(N)O(N)O(N) for N=2−2JN=2^{-2J}N=2−2J pixels.

Figure 4.16. Steps of the anisotropic wavelet transform.

4.5.2 Isotropic Wavelets¶

The anisotropic atoms (4.12) have independent scales in the two coordinate directions. For compactly supported wavelets, their supports lie in axis-aligned rectangles of size proportional to 2j1×2j22^{j_1}\times2^{j_2}2j1​×2j2​. This directional bias can produce visible artifacts in denoising and compression when it does not match the image geometry.

Figure 4.17. Anisotropic (left) versus isotropic (right) wavelet coefficients.

An alternative uses a common scale in both directions. Tensor products of one-dimensional approximation spaces give a two-dimensional multiresolution

We write

VjO:=Vj⊗VjV_j^O \mathrel{:=}V_j \otimes V_jVjO​:=Vj​⊗Vj​

for this isotropic 2-D approximation space.

Each step separates fine-scale approximation coefficients into three detail arrays and a coarse approximation:

aj−1⟼(aj,djH,djV,djD).a_{j-1} \longmapsto (a_j, d_j^H, d_j^V, d_j^D).aj−1​⟼(aj​,djH​,djV​,djD​).

As in one dimension, this map is orthogonal. It is implemented by applying the filtering and sub-sampling formula (4.8) in each coordinate direction.

One first applies 1-D horizontal filtering and sub-sampling

a~j=(aj−1⋆Hhˉ)↓H2d~j=(aj−1⋆Hgˉ)↓H2,\begin{aligned} \tilde a_j &= ( a_{j-1} \star^H \bar h ) \downarrow^H 2\\ \tilde d_j &= (a_{j-1}\star^H\bar g) \downarrow^H 2, \end{aligned}a~j​d~j​​=(aj−1​⋆Hhˉ)↓H2=(aj−1​⋆Hgˉ​)↓H2,​

where ⋆H\star^H⋆H denotes convolution along the first coordinate (called horizontal here), applied to each column of the array

a⋆Hbn1,n2=∑m1=0P−1an1−m1,n2bm1a \star^H b_{n_1,n_2} = \sum_{m_1=0}^{P-1} a_{n_1-m_1,n_2} b_{m_1}a⋆Hbn1​,n2​​=m1​=0∑P−1​an1​−m1​,n2​​bm1​​

Here a∈CP×Pa\in\mathbb{C}^{P\times P}a∈CP×P is a matrix and b∈CPb\in\mathbb{C}^Pb∈CP is a filter. The notation ↓H2\downarrow^H 2↓H2 denotes sub-sampling in the horizontal direction

(a↓H2)n1,n2=a2n1,n2.(a \downarrow^H 2)_{n_1,n_2} = a_{2n_1,n_2}.(a↓H2)n1​,n2​​=a2n1​,n2​​.

One then applies 1-D vertical filtering and sub-sampling to a~j\tilde a_ja~j​ and d~j\tilde d_jd~j​ to obtain

aj=(a~j⋆Vhˉ)↓V2,djV=(a~j⋆Vgˉ)↓V2,djH=(d~j⋆Vhˉ)↓V2,djD=(d~j⋆Vgˉ)↓V2,\begin{aligned} \begin{array}{ll} a_j &= ( \tilde a_j \star^V \bar h ) \downarrow^V 2,\\ d_j^V &= ( \tilde a_j \star^V \bar g ) \downarrow^V 2, \end{array}\qquad \begin{array}{ll} d_j^H &= ( \tilde d_j \star^V \bar h ) \downarrow^V 2,\\ d_j^D &= ( \tilde d_j \star^V \bar g ) \downarrow^V 2, \end{array} \end{aligned}aj​djV​​=(a~j​⋆Vhˉ)↓V2,=(a~j​⋆Vgˉ​)↓V2,​djH​djD​​=(d~j​⋆Vhˉ)↓V2,=(d~j​⋆Vgˉ​)↓V2,​​

where the vertical operators are defined analogously to the horizontal operators, acting on rows.

Fast 2-D wavelet transform.

The 2-D FWT algorithm iterates these steps through the scales:

  • Initialization: aJ=fa_J = faJ​=f.

    a~j=(aj−1⋆Hhˉ)↓H2,d~j=(aj−1⋆Hgˉ)↓H2,aj=(a~j⋆Vhˉ)↓V2,djV=(a~j⋆Vgˉ)↓V2,djH=(d~j⋆Vhˉ)↓V2,djD=(d~j⋆Vgˉ)↓V2.\begin{array}{ll} \tilde a_j &= ( a_{j-1} \star^H \bar h ) \downarrow^H 2, \\ \tilde d_j &= (a_{j-1}\star^H\bar g) \downarrow^H 2, \\ a_j &= ( \tilde a_j \star^V \bar h ) \downarrow^V 2, \end{array}\qquad \begin{array}{ll} d_j^V &= ( \tilde a_j \star^V \bar g ) \downarrow^V 2,\\ d_j^H &= ( \tilde d_j \star^V \bar h ) \downarrow^V 2,\\ d_j^D &= ( \tilde d_j \star^V \bar g ) \downarrow^V 2. \end{array}a~j​d~j​aj​​=(aj−1​⋆Hhˉ)↓H2,=(aj−1​⋆Hgˉ​)↓H2,=(a~j​⋆Vhˉ)↓V2,​djV​djH​djD​​=(a~j​⋆Vgˉ​)↓V2,=(d~j​⋆Vhˉ)↓V2,=(d~j​⋆Vgˉ​)↓V2.​

Fast 2-D inverse wavelet transform.

The inverse transform undoes the horizontal and vertical filtering steps. The first step computes

a~j=(aj↑V2)⋆Vh+(djV↑V2)⋆Vg,d~j=(djH↑V2)⋆Vh+(djD↑V2)⋆Vg,\begin{aligned} \tilde a_j &= (a_j\uparrow^V2)\star^Vh + (d_j^V\uparrow^V2)\star^Vg,\\ \tilde d_j &= (d_j^H\uparrow^V2)\star^Vh + (d_j^D\uparrow^V2)\star^Vg, \end{aligned}a~j​d~j​​=(aj​↑V2)⋆Vh+(djV​↑V2)⋆Vg,=(djH​↑V2)⋆Vh+(djD​↑V2)⋆Vg,​

aj−1=(a~j↑H2)⋆Hh+(d~j↑H2)⋆Hg.\begin{aligned} a_{j-1} &= (\tilde a_j\uparrow^H2)\star^Hh + (\tilde d_j\uparrow^H2)\star^Hg. \end{aligned}aj−1​​=(a~j​↑H2)⋆Hh+(d~j​↑H2)⋆Hg.​

4.6 Wavelet Design¶

Implementing the FWT requires the filters hhh and ggg, rather than explicit formulas for the scaling function φ\varphiφ and wavelet ψ\psiψ. Most useful wavelets have no elementary closed form; their refinement equations define them implicitly, and the cascade algorithm approximates them.

This section derives constraints on the filters and gives examples. Under the usual quadrature-mirror construction, the low-pass filter hhh determines the high-pass filter ggg.

4.6.1 Low-pass Filter Constraints¶

We introduce the following three conditions on a filter hhh

h^(0)=2(C1)\begin{aligned} \hat h(0)&=\sqrt{2} \end{aligned} \tag{$C_1$}h^(0)​=2​​(C1​)
∣h^(ω)∣2+∣h^(ω+π)∣2=2,(C2)\begin{aligned} |\hat h(\omega)|^2 + |\hat h(\omega+\pi)|^2&=2, \end{aligned} \tag{$C_2$}∣h^(ω)∣2+∣h^(ω+π)∣2​=2,​(C2​)
inf⁡ω∈[−π/2,π/2]∣h^(ω)∣>0.(C∗)\begin{aligned} \underset{\omega\in [-\pi/2,\pi/2]}{\inf} |\hat h(\omega)|&>0. \end{aligned} \tag{$C^*$}ω∈[−π/2,π/2]inf​∣h^(ω)∣​>0.​(C∗)

These conditions use the Fourier series of the filter h∈RZh \in \mathbb{R}^\mathbb{Z}h∈RZ:

∀ω∈R/2πZ,h^(ω):=∑n∈Zhne−inω.(4.13)\forall \omega\in \mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}, \quad \hat h(\omega) \mathrel{:=}\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} h_n e^{-\mathrm{i}n \omega}. \tag{4.13}∀ω∈R/2πZ,h^(ω):=n∈Z∑​hn​e−inω.(4.13)

If h∈ℓ1(Z)h \in \ell^1(\mathbb{Z})h∈ℓ1(Z), this defines a continuous periodic function h^∈C0(R/2πZ)\hat h \in \mathcal{C}^0(\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z})h^∈C0(R/2πZ), and the definition extends to h∈ℓ2(Z)h \in \ell^2(\mathbb{Z})h∈ℓ2(Z) to give h^∈L2(R/2πZ)\hat h \in L^2(\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z})h^∈L2(R/2πZ).

Theorem 4.4

If an integrable real scaling function φ\varphiφ defines a multiresolution analysis and its filter hhh is summable, then (C1C_1C1​) and (C2C_2C2​) hold for hhh defined in (4.7).

Conversely, if a finitely supported real filter hhh satisfies (C1C_1C1​), (C2C_2C2​), and (C∗C^*C∗), then there exists a φ\varphiφ defining multi-resolution approximation spaces whose associated filter is hhh as defined in (4.7).

Proof

We prove the forward implication. The converse requires a separate construction.

We now prove condition (C1C_1C1​).

The refinement equation convolves a function on the real line with a discrete filter, represented by a sum of Dirac masses:

12φ(t2)=∑n∈Zhnφ(t−n).(4.14)\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \varphi\left( \frac{t}{2} \right) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} h_n \varphi(t-n). \tag{4.14}2​1​φ(2t​)=n∈Z∑​hn​φ(t−n).(4.14)

Writing h⋆φh \star \varphih⋆φ for this convolution and assuming h∈ℓ1(Z)h \in \ell_1(\mathbb{Z})h∈ℓ1​(Z) and φ∈L1(R)\varphi\in L^1(\mathbb{R})φ∈L1(R), Fubini’s theorem shows that h⋆φ∈L1(R)h \star \varphi\in L^1(\mathbb{R})h⋆φ∈L1(R) and gives

F(∑n∈Zhnφ(t−n))(ω)=∫R∑n∈Zhnφ(t−n)e−iωtdt=∑n∈Zhn∫Rφ(t−n)e−iωtdt=∑n∈Zhne−inω∫Rφ(x)e−iωxdx=φ^(ω)h^(ω)\begin{aligned} \mathcal{F}( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} h_n \varphi(t-n) )(\omega) &= \int_\mathbb{R}\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} h_n \varphi(t-n) e^{-\mathrm{i}\omega t} \mathrm{d}t = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} h_n \int_\mathbb{R}\varphi(t-n) e^{-\mathrm{i}\omega t} \mathrm{d}t \\ & = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} h_n e^{-\mathrm{i}n \omega} \int_\mathbb{R}\varphi(x) e^{-\mathrm{i}\omega x} \mathrm{d}x = \hat \varphi(\omega) \hat h(\omega) \end{aligned}F(n∈Z∑​hn​φ(t−n))(ω)​=∫R​n∈Z∑​hn​φ(t−n)e−iωtdt=n∈Z∑​hn​∫R​φ(t−n)e−iωtdt=n∈Z∑​hn​e−inω∫R​φ(x)e−iωxdx=φ^​(ω)h^(ω)​

where we substituted x=t−nx = t-nx=t−n. Here h^(ω)\hat h(\omega)h^(ω) is the 2π2\pi2π-periodic Fourier series of the filter, defined in (4.13), while φ^(ω)\hat\varphi(\omega)φ^​(ω) is the continuous Fourier transform of the scaling function. The product therefore combines a 2π2\pi2π-periodic factor h^\hat hh^ with a generally nonperiodic factor φ^\hat \varphiφ^​.

We recall that F(f(⋅/s))=sf^(s⋅)\mathcal{F}(f(\cdot/s)) = s \hat f(s \cdot)F(f(⋅/s))=sf^​(s⋅).

In the Fourier domain, equation (4.14) thus reads

φ^(2ω)=12h^(ω)φ^(ω).(4.15)\hat\varphi(2\omega) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat h(\omega) \hat \varphi(\omega). \tag{4.15}φ^​(2ω)=2​1​h^(ω)φ^​(ω).(4.15)

One can show that φ^(0)≠0\hat \varphi(0) \neq 0φ^​(0)=0 (actually, ∣φ^(0)∣=1|\hat \varphi(0)| = 1∣φ^​(0)∣=1), so that this relation implies the first condition (C1C_1C1​).

We now prove condition (C2C_2C2​).

The orthogonality of {φ(⋅−n)}n\{\varphi(\cdot-n)\}_n{φ(⋅−n)}n​ can be expressed as a continuous convolution (see also Proposition 4.1)

∀ n∈Z,(φ⋆φˉ)(n)=δn,0\forall \,n \in \mathbb{Z}, \quad (\varphi\star\bar\varphi)(n)=\delta_{n,0}∀n∈Z,(φ⋆φˉ​)(n)=δn,0​

where φˉ(x)=φ(−x)\bar \varphi(x) = \varphi(-x)φˉ​(x)=φ(−x), and thus in the Fourier domain, using (4.15) which shows φ^(ω)=12h^(ω/2)φ^(ω/2)\hat\varphi(\omega) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat h(\omega/2) \hat \varphi(\omega/2)φ^​(ω)=2​1​h^(ω/2)φ^​(ω/2)

1=∑k∣φ^(ω+2kπ)∣2=12∑k∣h^(ω/2+kπ)∣2∣φ^(ω/2+kπ)∣2.1 = \sum_k |\hat \varphi(\omega+2k\pi)|^2 = \frac{1}{2}\sum_k |\hat h(\omega/2+k\pi)|^2 |\hat \varphi(\omega/2+k\pi)|^2.1=k∑​∣φ^​(ω+2kπ)∣2=21​k∑​∣h^(ω/2+kπ)∣2∣φ^​(ω/2+kπ)∣2.

Since h^\hat hh^ is 2π2\pi2π-periodic, one can separate even and odd indices kkk and obtain

2=∣h^(ω/2)∣2∑k∣φ^(ω/2+2kπ)∣2+∣h^(ω/2+π)∣2∑k∣φ^(ω/2+2kπ+π)∣22 = |\hat h(\omega/2)|^2 \sum_k |\hat \varphi(\omega/2+2k\pi)|^2 + |\hat h(\omega/2+\pi)|^2 \sum_k |\hat \varphi(\omega/2+2k\pi+\pi)|^22=∣h^(ω/2)∣2k∑​∣φ^​(ω/2+2kπ)∣2+∣h^(ω/2+π)∣2k∑​∣φ^​(ω/2+2kπ+π)∣2

To obtain condition (C2C_2C2​), apply ∑k∣φ^(ω+2kπ)∣2=1\sum_k |\hat \varphi(\omega+2k\pi)|^2=1∑k​∣φ^​(ω+2kπ)∣2=1 at ω′=ω/2\omega'=\omega/2ω′=ω/2 instead of ω\omegaω:

∣h^(ω′)∣2+∣h^(ω′+π)∣2=2.|\hat h(\omega')|^2+|\hat h(\omega'+\pi)|^2 = 2.∣h^(ω′)∣2+∣h^(ω′+π)∣2=2.

The converse requires constructing a scaling function φ\varphiφ from the filter hhh; we do not prove it here. Iterating (4.15) suggests the infinite-product construction

φ^(ω)=∏k=1∞h^(ω/2k)2.(4.16)\hat \varphi(\omega) = \prod_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{\hat h(\omega/2^k)}{\sqrt{2}}. \tag{4.16}φ^​(ω)=k=1∏∞​2​h^(ω/2k)​.(4.16)

Condition (C∗C^*C∗) can be shown to imply that this infinite product converges and defines a (non-periodic) function in L2(R)L^2(\mathbb{R})L2(R).

Condition (C∗C^*C∗) prevents zeros of h^\hat hh^ on the central half-period. It is a sufficient nondegeneracy condition for the converse construction used here.

4.6.2 High-pass Filter Constraints¶

We now introduce the following two conditions on a pair of filters (g,h)(g,h)(g,h)

∣g^(ω)∣2+∣g^(ω+π)∣2=2(C3)\begin{aligned} |\hat g(\omega)|^2 + |\hat g(\omega+\pi)|^2&=2 \end{aligned} \tag{$C_3$}∣g^​(ω)∣2+∣g^​(ω+π)∣2​=2​(C3​)
g^(ω)h^(ω)∗+g^(ω+π)h^(ω+π)∗=0.(C4)\begin{aligned} \hat g(\omega) \hat h(\omega)^* + \hat g(\omega+\pi) \hat h(\omega+\pi)^*&=0. \end{aligned} \tag{$C_4$}g^​(ω)h^(ω)∗+g^​(ω+π)h^(ω+π)∗​=0.​(C4​)

Figure 4.25 illustrates these filter constraints.

Figure 4.25. Constraints on low-pass and high-pass filters.

Theorem 4.5

If (φ,ψ)(\varphi,\psi)(φ,ψ) defines a multi-resolution analysis, then (C3C_3C3​) and (C4C_4C4​) hold for (h,g)(h,g)(h,g) defined in (4.7).

Conversely, if the finitely supported real low-pass filter satisfies (C1C_1C1​)–(C∗C^*C∗), and a summable real filter ggg satisfies (C3C_3C3​)–(C4C_4C4​), then there is a multiresolution wavelet pair (φ,ψ)(\varphi,\psi)(φ,ψ) whose associated filters are (h,g)(h,g)(h,g) as defined in (4.7). Furthermore,

ψ^(ω)=12g^(ω/2)φ^(ω/2).(4.17)\hat \psi(\omega) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \hat g(\omega/2) \hat \varphi(\omega/2). \tag{4.17}ψ^​(ω)=2​1​g^​(ω/2)φ^​(ω/2).(4.17)
Proof

We prove the forward implication, beginning with condition (C3C_3C3​).

The refinement equation for the wavelet reads

12ψ(t2)=∑n∈Zgnφ(t−n)\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \psi\left( \frac{t}{2} \right) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} g_n \varphi(t-n)2​1​ψ(2t​)=n∈Z∑​gn​φ(t−n)

and thus in the Fourier domain

ψ^(2ω)=12g^(ω)φ^(ω).(4.18)\hat\psi(2\omega) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat g(\omega) \hat \varphi(\omega). \tag{4.18}ψ^​(2ω)=2​1​g^​(ω)φ^​(ω).(4.18)

Orthogonality of the translates {ψ(⋅−n)}n\{ \psi(\cdot-n) \}_n{ψ(⋅−n)}n​ gives

∀ n∈Z,(ψ⋆ψˉ)(n)=δn,0\forall \,n \in \mathbb{Z}, \quad (\psi\star\bar\psi)(n)=\delta_{n,0}∀n∈Z,(ψ⋆ψˉ​)(n)=δn,0​

and thus in the Fourier domain (using Poisson’s formula, see also Proposition 4.1)

∑k∣ψ^(ω+2kπ)∣2=1.\sum_k |\hat \psi(\omega+2k\pi)|^2 = 1.k∑​∣ψ^​(ω+2kπ)∣2=1.

Apply the Fourier refinement equation (4.18) and separate the even and odd terms, as in the proof of condition (C2C_2C2​) in Theorem 4.4. This gives condition (C3C_3C3​).

Figure 4.25 shows the squared Fourier magnitudes of a pair of filters satisfying this complementarity condition.

We now prove condition (C4C_4C4​).

The orthogonality between {ψ(⋅−n)}n\{ \psi(\cdot-n) \}_n{ψ(⋅−n)}n​ and {φ(⋅−n)}n\{ \varphi(\cdot-n) \}_n{φ(⋅−n)}n​ is written as

∀ n∈Z,ψ⋆φˉ(n)=0\forall \,n \in \mathbb{Z}, \quad \psi \star \bar \varphi(n)=0∀n∈Z,ψ⋆φˉ​(n)=0

and hence in the Fourier domain (using Poisson’s formula, similarly to Proposition 4.1)

∑kψ^(ω+2kπ)φ^∗(ω+2kπ)=0.\sum_k \hat \psi(\omega+2k\pi)\hat \varphi^*(\omega+2k\pi) = 0.k∑​ψ^​(ω+2kπ)φ^​∗(ω+2kπ)=0.

Using the Fourier domain refinement equations (4.15) and (4.18), this is equivalent to condition (C4C_4C4​).

Quadrature mirror filters.

Quadrature mirror filters (QMF) define ggg as a function of hhh so that the conditions of Theorem 4.5 are automatically satisfied. Most wavelet constructions implicitly use this choice (other phase choices can yield different wavelets spanning the same detail spaces).

Proposition 4.6

For a real filter h∈ℓ1(Z)h\in\ell^1(\mathbb{Z})h∈ℓ1(Z) satisfying (C2C_2C2​), the filter g∈ℓ2(Z)g \in \ell^2(\mathbb{Z})g∈ℓ2(Z) defined by

∀ n∈Z,gn=(−1)1−nh1−n(4.19)\forall \,n \in \mathbb{Z}, \quad g_n = (-1)^{1-n}h_{1-n} \tag{4.19}∀n∈Z,gn​=(−1)1−nh1−n​(4.19)

satisfies conditions (C3C_3C3​) and (C4C_4C4​).

Proof

Taking the Fourier series of the defining relation gives

g^(ω)=e−iωh^(ω+π)∗,(4.20)\hat g(\omega) = e^{-i \omega} \hat h(\omega+\pi)^*, \tag{4.20}g^​(ω)=e−iωh^(ω+π)∗,(4.20)

so that

∣g^(ω)∣2+∣g^(ω+π)∣2=∣e−iωh^(ω+π)∗∣2+∣e−i(ω+π)h^(ω+2π)∗∣2=∣h^(ω+π)∣2+∣h^(ω+2π)∣2=2.|\hat g(\omega)|^2 + |\hat g(\omega+\pi)|^2 = |e^{-i \omega} \hat h(\omega+\pi)^*|^2 + |e^{-i (\omega+\pi)} \hat h(\omega+2\pi)^*|^2 = |\hat h(\omega+\pi)|^2 + |\hat h(\omega+2\pi)|^2 = 2.∣g^​(ω)∣2+∣g^​(ω+π)∣2=∣e−iωh^(ω+π)∗∣2+∣e−i(ω+π)h^(ω+2π)∗∣2=∣h^(ω+π)∣2+∣h^(ω+2π)∣2=2.

where we used the fact that h^\hat hh^ is 2π2\pi2π-periodic, and also

g^(ω)h^(ω)∗+g^(ω+π)h^(ω+π)∗=e−iωh^(ω+π)∗h^(ω)∗+e−i(ω+π)h^(ω+2π)∗h^(ω+π)∗=(e−iω+e−i(ω+π))h^(ω+π)∗h^(ω)∗=0.\begin{aligned} \hat g(\omega) \hat h(\omega)^* + \hat g(\omega+\pi) \hat h(\omega+\pi)^* &= e^{-i \omega} \hat h(\omega+\pi)^* \hat h(\omega)^* + e^{-i (\omega+\pi)} \hat h(\omega+2\pi)^* \hat h(\omega+\pi)^* \\ &= (e^{-i \omega}+e^{-i (\omega+\pi)}) \hat h(\omega+\pi)^* \hat h(\omega)^* =0. \end{aligned}g^​(ω)h^(ω)∗+g^​(ω+π)h^(ω+π)∗​=e−iωh^(ω+π)∗h^(ω)∗+e−i(ω+π)h^(ω+2π)∗h^(ω+π)∗=(e−iω+e−i(ω+π))h^(ω+π)∗h^(ω)∗=0.​

4.6.3 Wavelet Design Constraints¶

One can construct a multiresolution wavelet pair by designing a finite filter hhh satisfying (C1C_1C1​)–(C∗C^*C∗). The scaling function is obtained through the infinite product (4.16). Except in special cases such as Haar wavelets, it has no elementary closed form. The QMF relation (4.19) then defines ggg, and (4.17) defines ψ\psiψ.

Fourier atoms are fixed exponentials, whereas mother wavelets can be designed to meet several requirements:

  • Size of the support.

  • Cancellation of polynomials, measured by the number ppp of vanishing moments.

  • Symmetry (for compactly supported scalar orthogonal wavelets, the Haar system is the exceptional symmetric case).

  • Smoothness (number of derivatives).

We now explain how these design requirements interact with conditions (C1C_1C1​)–(C4C_4C4​).

Vanishing moments.

A wavelet ψ\psiψ has ppp vanishing moments if

∀ k=0,…,p−1,∫Rψ(x) xkdx=0.(4.21)\forall \,k=0,\ldots,p-1, \quad \int_\mathbb{R}\psi(x) \, x^k \mathrm{d}x = 0. \tag{4.21}∀k=0,…,p−1,∫R​ψ(x)xkdx=0.(4.21)

Vanishing moments make ⟨f, ψj,n⟩\langle f,\,\psi_{j,n}\rangle⟨f,ψj,n​⟩ small when fff has regularity Cα\text{C}^\alphaCα with α<p\alpha<pα<p on Supp(ψj,n)(\psi_{j,n})(ψj,n​). A Taylor expansion of fff about 2jn2^j n2jn on the wavelet’s support explains this cancellation.

The vanishing-moment condition has the following equivalent Fourier characterization; see Figure 4.26.

Figure 4.26. Vanishing moments correspond to vanishing derivatives of the Fourier transform.

Proposition 4.7

Assuming the required moments of ψ\psiψ and derivatives of the filter symbols exist, a wavelet obtained by the QMF construction (4.19) has ppp vanishing moments if and only if

∀ k=0,…,p−1,dkh^dωk(π)=dkg^dωk(0)=0.(4.22)\forall \,k=0,\ldots,p-1, \quad \frac{\mathrm{d}^k \hat h}{\mathrm{d}\omega^k}(\pi) = \frac{\mathrm{d}^k \hat g}{\mathrm{d}\omega^k}(0) = 0. \tag{4.22}∀k=0,…,p−1,dωkdkh^​(π)=dωkdkg^​​(0)=0.(4.22)

Relations (4.17) and (4.19) imply

and differentiating this relation shows

2ψ^(1)(2ω)=h^(ω+π)∗ρ(1)(ω)+h^(1)(ω+π)∗ρ(ω)2 \hat \psi^{(1)}(2\omega) = \hat h(\omega+\pi)^* \rho^{(1)}(\omega) + \hat h^{(1)}(\omega+\pi)^* \rho(\omega)2ψ^​(1)(2ω)=h^(ω+π)∗ρ(1)(ω)+h^(1)(ω+π)∗ρ(ω)

Conditions (C1C_1C1​) and (C2C_2C2​) give h^(π)=0\hat h(\pi)=0h^(π)=0, so every admissible wavelet has at least 1 vanishing moment: ∫ψ=0\int \psi=0∫ψ=0. By (4.22), additional vanishing moments require the Fourier transform h^\hat hh^ to vanish to higher order at ω=π\omega=\piω=π.

Support.

Figure 4.27 shows the wavelet coefficients of a piecewise smooth signal. The cancellation provided by ψ\psiψ suppresses coefficients in smooth regions, leaving the largest coefficients near singularities.

Figure 4.27. Location of large coefficients for Haar (left) and Daubechies-4 (right) wavelets applied to the same piecewise-smooth signal.

Choosing ψ\psiψ with short support limits how many wavelets intersect each singularity.

One can show that the size of the support of ψ\psiψ is proportional to the size of the support of hhh.

Short support competes with the vanishing-moment requirement (4.21). Indeed, one can prove that for an orthogonal wavelet basis with ppp vanishing moments

∣Supp(ψ)∣⩾2p−1,|\text{Supp}(\psi)| \geqslant 2p-1,∣Supp(ψ)∣⩾2p−1,

where the left-hand side denotes the length of the smallest closed interval containing the support of a compactly supported orthogonal mother wavelet.

Chapter 5 studies in detail the tradeoff between support size and vanishing moments in nonlinear approximation of piecewise smooth signals.

Smoothness.

In compression or denoising applications, an approximate signal is recovered from a partial set IMI_MIM​ of coefficients,

fM=∑(j,n)∈IM⟨f, ψj,n⟩ψj,n.f_M = \sum_{(j,n) \in I_M} \langle f,\,\psi_{j,n}\rangle \psi_{j,n}.fM​=(j,n)∈IM​∑​⟨f,ψj,n​⟩ψj,n​.

This finite sum is at least as smooth as ψ\psiψ.

A smooth wavelet ψ\psiψ helps avoid visible reconstruction artifacts. Smoothness controls the regularity of the reconstructed signal, while vanishing moments and localization primarily determine the approximation rates studied below. These properties are often linked: in many families, including the Daubechies wavelets introduced next, more vanishing moments also bring greater smoothness.

4.6.4 Daubechies Wavelets¶

To build a wavelet ψ\psiψ with a fixed number ppp of vanishing moments, one designs the filter hhh, and uses the quadrature mirror filter relation (4.19) to compute ggg. One therefore looks for hhh such that

∣h^(ω)∣2+∣h^(ω+π)∣2=2,h^(0)=2,and∀ k=0,…,p−1,  dkh^dωk(π)=0.|\hat h(\omega)|^2 + |\hat h(\omega+\pi)|^2 = 2, \quad \hat h(0)=\sqrt{2}, \quad \text{and} \quad \forall \,k=0,\ldots,p-1, \; {\frac{\mathrm{d}^k \hat h}{\mathrm{d}\omega^k} }(\pi)=0.∣h^(ω)∣2+∣h^(ω+π)∣2=2,h^(0)=2​,and∀k=0,…,p−1,dωkdkh^​(π)=0.

These conditions give algebraic relations between the coefficients of hhh, which can be solved explicitly using the Euclidean division algorithm for polynomials.

The resulting Daubechies wavelets have ppp vanishing moments and attain the minimum support length 2p−12p-12p−1 among compactly supported orthogonal wavelets.
